passages.texte: Esteban Beretti-Prenant is data scientist · ai engineer. I put decision models in anyone's hands. Data scientist. I port foresight models out of Excel and into the browser, build the pipelines that feed them, and check every port against the original. Measured drift: 0.00002%.

A suite of foresight simulators. Four transition models, ported from Excel to the browser. Four self-contained web applications that replay 2050 foresight models for energy, mobility, agriculture and digital infrastructure, in the browser, with no server involved.
A suite of foresight simulators covers these domains: Modelling, Model porting, Data visualisation.

A suite of foresight simulators. Context: The teams worked from Excel workbooks running to dozens of sheets, backed by Power BI dashboards. Looking up a scenario meant having the workbook, the right version of it, a licence, and knowing how to re-run the macros. Results circulated as screenshots. My brief: make those models something anyone could open and manipulate from a browser.

On the project « A suite of foresight simulators » (2026), my role: Design and development, as an apprentice at a public research institute. Technologies used: JavaScript, Python, openpyxl, Chart.js, noUiSlider, Design system DSFR.

Constraints on the project « A suite of foresight simulators » : No application server: deliverables had to be emailable and openable offline. Non-negotiable fidelity to the source model. A simulator that diverges from the workbook is worse than useless: it creates a second truth. No sensitive source data and no original workbook committed to the repositories. A mandated design system, shared across all four tools.

Technical decision on « A suite of foresight simulators » : Port the workbook formulas to JavaScript rather than pre-compute every scenario. Reason: Pre-computing would have frozen the tool on the handful of reference scenarios. Porting the model makes the free scenario genuinely editable: move one parameter and the whole chain recalculates, with no trip back through Excel.

Technical decision on « A suite of foresight simulators » : Verify the port automatically, and fail the data generation past 0.1% drift. Reason: It is the only way to keep the fidelity promise over time. The generator replays the reference trajectories through the ported model and compares them sheet by sheet. Observed drift: 0.00002%.

Technical decision on « A suite of foresight simulators » : Build-free JavaScript, with modules loaded in script-tag order. Reason: The «single file, openable offline» constraint ruled out a bundler. The cost is a load order to respect: small, and documented. The benefit is a deliverable that survives any workstation it lands on.

Technical decision on « A suite of foresight simulators » : Treat an empty field as «follow the baseline trend», not as zero. Reason: That is the source model's own convention. Without it, opening free mode would have frozen all 93 crops at their starting level, making the baseline trajectory unreachable from the very screen meant to extend it.

Results of the project « A suite of foresight simulators » : Four simulators in service, usable with no licence and no installation. Reference scenarios are explorable by non-specialists, while expert parameters stay available behind a dedicated mode. Every deliverable exists in two forms: a self-contained HTML file for sending by email, and a hosted version. Regenerating the data from the workbook is scripted, verified and reproducible. A publishable version of one of the four simulators is playable on this site, with its data entirely regenerated.

Key figures for « A suite of foresight simulators » : 0.00002% drift from the source model (measured automatically; the build fails past 0.1%) ; 4 domains covered (energy, mobility, agriculture, digital) ; 93 configurable crops (in the agriculture module alone) ; 0 servers required (a single HTML file is enough)

The platform that hosts them. Public site and shared foundation for the simulators. A Next.js site that presents the team's work and hosts the simulators, built on a shared component foundation with hand-written WebGL backgrounds.
The platform that hosts them covers these domains: Web development, Design system, WebGL.

The platform that hosts them. Context: The simulators existed, but each on its own, with no shared front door and nothing tying them together. What was needed was a site that explained the approach, opened access to the tools, and served as a reusable base for whatever came next.

On the project « The platform that hosts them » (2026), my role: Design and development, as an apprentice at a public research institute. Technologies used: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript strict, Tailwind CSS v4, Radix UI, motion, GLSL, Chart.js, zod, Vitest, Playwright, Vercel.

Constraints on the project « The platform that hosts them » : Respect a mandated visual identity, colour tokens included. Interface, content and code comments in French. Stay simple to host, with no dedicated infrastructure.

Technical decision on « The platform that hosts them » : Write the animated backgrounds in GLSL instead of importing a 3D library. Reason: The backgrounds needed no scene, no camera and no model loader. A shader on a full-screen quad does the job for a fraction of the weight, and stays readable.

Technical decision on « The platform that hosts them » : One single source of truth for the site's identity. Reason: The previous version repeated the production domain across eleven HTML pages: canonical tags, Open Graph, sitemap, robots. A single module now exports all of it, so there is no longer a value left behind when something changes.

Technical decision on « The platform that hosts them » : Move the four domains out of the main navigation. Reason: At eight items the bar reached roughly 1150 px and overlapped the logo between 1024 and 1150 px. The pages are still served and still indexed; only the route in changes.

Results of the project « The platform that hosts them » : A single front door to all four simulators. A component foundation reused by the tools that followed. Continuous deployment on every merge to the main branch.
Key figures for « The platform that hosts them » : 4 simulators hosted ; 0 3D dependencies for the backgrounds (hand-written GLSL shaders) ; TS strict (types checked in continuous integration)

Global flows of critical minerals. Twenty-five years of customs declarations, queryable offline. A supply-chain analysis application for critical raw materials, backed by a three-stage pipeline: bulk extraction from the United Nations API, cleaning and export to Parquet, then querying entirely in the browser through DuckDB-WASM.
Global flows of critical minerals covers these domains: Data engineering, Analytics, Data visualisation.

Global flows of critical minerals. Context: Analysing critical-material supply chains means cross-referencing bilateral customs declarations across two decades. The source API is paid and rate-limited, and the volumes exceed what a spreadsheet can absorb. What was needed was a pipeline that extracts once, cleanly, and an interface that then queries without ever asking again.

On the project « Global flows of critical minerals » (2026), my role: Sole owner: design, pipeline, data model and interface. Technologies used: Python, DuckDB, Apache Parquet, DuckDB-WASM, JavaScript, Three.js, Leaflet, Chart.js, Vercel.

Constraints on the project « Global flows of critical minerals » : Paid, rate-limited API: never re-download a (reporter, year) pair already retrieved. A full extraction runs for hours and will be interrupted. Resuming has to be automatic. The analysis had to stay usable with no backend, therefore with no hosting cost and no data exposure.

Technical decision on « Global flows of critical minerals » : A checkpoint on disk, consulted before every call. Reason: Completed pairs and permanent failures are journalled separately. An interruption picks up on the next run, and failures replay on their own, after five attempts with exponential backoff.

Technical decision on « Global flows of critical minerals » : Partitioned Parquet rather than a served database. Reason: The columnar format reads in chunks straight from static storage. Combined with DuckDB-WASM, it yields interactive analysis without a single machine to maintain.

Technical decision on « Global flows of critical minerals » : Distribute the datasets through the repository's releases. Reason: The files exceed what a Git repository should carry, and the site's static hosting is not built for it. Releases version the data the way the repository versions the pipeline.

Results of the project « Global flows of critical minerals » : Five analytical angles: value chains, country-to-country dependencies, material origin, ore comparison, and detailed product tracking. Dedicated handling of critical materials, with pre-aggregation and a bilateral view. Application deployed and publicly available.

Key figures for « Global flows of critical minerals » : 240 reporting countries ; 2000-2025 years of history ; 97 product chapters (2-digit Harmonized System classification) ; 100% of queries run client-side (no data ever leaves the browser)

A RAG system written by hand. Understanding retrieval-augmented generation by building it without a framework. A retrieval-augmented system written from scratch in Python (embeddings, cosine similarity, local generation), deliberately without an orchestration library, in order to own every layer of it.

passages.texte: Constraints on the project « A RAG system written by hand » : Run entirely locally, with no API key and no third-party service. Stay short enough to be read end to end and to work as teaching material.

passages.texte: Technical decision on « A RAG system written by hand » : Cosine similarity in NumPy rather than a vector database. Reason: At the scale of a personal corpus, a dot product over a matrix fits on one line and runs instantly. A vector database would have added a dependency, a service and an abstraction to solve a problem that does not exist yet.
passages.source: A RAG system written by hand

passages.texte: Technical decision on « A RAG system written by hand » : A compact embedding model and a local generation model. Reason: 384 dimensions are more than enough for personal document search, and the pair fits on an ordinary machine, which makes the project reproducible by anyone who clones it.
passages.source: A RAG system written by hand

passages.texte: Results of the project « A RAG system written by hand » : A working system in one readable file, with a guide that explains each component. The direct basis for this portfolio's own search engine: the same model, this time ported into the browser.
passages.source: A RAG system written by hand

What I hand over. Volume and repetition. Porting 106 rows of an expert table into a data structure, writing the seventh chart component on the same pattern, rolling a mechanical refactor through nine modules, producing a first draft of documentation from the code. These are tasks where mistakes are visible and verification is cheap. That is exactly where an agent pays for itself.

What I never hand over : Defining what counts as correct. Deciding that an empty field means «follow the baseline trend» and not «zero» is not a coding question: it is a reading of the domain model. Getting it wrong produces software that works perfectly and answers wrongly. Choosing which invariants to check. An agent will happily write the test you ask for. Knowing that the test that matters is the sheet-by-sheet comparison against the source workbook, and setting the failure threshold at 0.1%, is judgement, not generation. Trade-offs forced by the ground. Giving up a bundler because the deliverable has to open offline from an email attachment: that decision comes from the field, not from general best practice. Reading line by line whatever ships. I do not approve a diff I could not defend. If I cannot explain why a line is there, it does not stay.

The question I put to an agent is never «does this work?» but «how will I know when it has stopped working?». For the simulators, the answer lives in the data generator: it replays the reference trajectories through the JavaScript port, compares them against the workbook's outputs, and refuses to emit the dataset past 0.1% drift. It is that guardrail, not code review, that guarantees the simulator and the workbook will never say two different things. Drift observed in practice: 0.00002%.

Systems you only understand by running them. Everything below executes in your browser, on a canvas, with no library: a few hundred lines each, and nothing pre-computed. A network that learns : Backpropagation written by hand, with no library. Flock : Emergent behaviour from three local rules. k-means : Convergence, shown one iteration at a time. Agar : A playable system, held together by a single trade-off.
